intro: The first of Debussy’s three symphonic sketches is heard here in Lawrence Odom’s concert-band transcription, not the original orchestration. How do short figures and overlapping rhythms accumulate into its broad closing passage?
question: How do small figures grow into a broad ending?

cues.title: A low, quiet opening
cues.text: The opening builds from a quiet foundation in the low register. This is Lawrence Odom’s concert-band transcription: listen for how sustained sounds support the shorter figures, without expecting the string sections of Debussy’s original orchestration.
cues.evidence: The analysis finds a low relative level and predominantly low-frequency sound in the opening; Commons credits Odom’s band transcription.

cues.title: The sea from childhood
cues.text: Debussy visited Cannes during childhood summers and entered the Paris Conservatoire at ten. He began La Mer in 1903 and completed it in 1905; his attraction to the sea long preceded the score.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg’s Boston Symphony programme note records the childhood visits, Conservatoire entry and composition dates.

cues.title: Listen below the fragments
cues.text: Follow the sustained lower notes as well as the shorter gestures above them. These layers need not change at the same speed: a held foundation can support several turns of a melodic figure.
cues.evidence: This describes the layered writing of the introduction, without assigning a particular figure or instrument an entrance time.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Beyond the introduction
cues.text: The main span grows from short melodic ideas rather than one long, repeatedly restated tune. Across this stretch, listen for changes in rhythm and register that alter a figure without making it wholly unfamiliar.
cues.evidence: The score separates a slow introduction from the main span; an audio change near 1:42 supports only approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hokusai on the cover
cues.text: Debussy chose an adaptation of Hokusai’s The Great Wave off Kanagawa for the published score. The image belongs to the work’s own publication history, rather than a later record designer’s association.
cues.evidence: The Boston Symphony programme note identifies Debussy’s choice of Hokusai for the score’s publication.

cues.title: Two against three
cues.text: Throughout this movement, groups of two and three repeatedly share the same stretch of time. Listen for a figure that divides the beat differently from its neighbour: rhythmic friction need not require a faster underlying pulse.
cues.evidence: Jacob Greenberg’s Boston Symphony note identifies recurring interplay between groups of two and three in the first movement.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Activity and overall level
cues.text: In this stretch, listen for small, closely spaced gestures within a relatively quiet texture. The frequency of attacks and the strength of the overall sound are different features; try following one without losing the other.
cues.evidence: The analysis detects more attacks around 3:50–3:55, while the relative level remains well below the closing peak.

cues.title: A crest, then withdrawal
cues.text: This part of the movement contains a swell followed by a long retreat. Follow the whole rise and fall rather than treating the stronger passage as the start of an uninterrupted ascent to the ending.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls by about 25 dB across 4:35–5:05 before recovering.

cues.title: After the withdrawal
cues.text: Around this passage, the sound recovers from a pronounced low point. Listen for the length and shape of the renewed phrases, comparing them with the more fragmentary gestures heard earlier.
cues.evidence: The analysis identifies a strong change near 5:12 and an 18 dB rise in relative level across 5:05–5:15.

cues.title: Another change of scale
cues.text: The surrounding stretch builds in level and upper-frequency energy. Compare the longer musical line with the smaller gestures inside it: the two can grow at different rates.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises across 5:35–5:55, accompanied by a shift towards higher-frequency sound.

cues.title: Following the lower line
cues.text: Through this withdrawal, follow the lower part rather than only the highest melody. A sustained upper note can acquire a different harmonic role when the bass moves underneath it.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows a broad fall in level around 6:15–6:30; the bass-line invitation does not claim a machine-identified chord change.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The first audience
cues.text: Camille Chevillard conducted the Lamoureux Orchestra in the premiere on 15 October 1905. Reception improved when Debussy conducted the work himself in Paris in January 1908.
cues.evidence: The Boston Symphony programme note supplies the premiere details and contrasts the reception in 1905 and 1908.

cues.title: Towards the broad ending
cues.text: The final span builds out of the preceding quiet passage. Listen for how sustained phrases gather weight before the largest peak, rather than hearing every increase as a separate climax.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises through 8:05–8:20, before the recording’s strongest sustained passage at 8:30–8:50.

cues.title: Broad chords, smaller movement
cues.text: Near the close, compare the broad chordal writing with the smaller movement inside it. This is the first sketch’s “noon”, not the end of the three-part work; the band transcription carries the same large-scale destination.
cues.evidence: The first movement’s score has a broad concluding passage; the analysis locates the strongest sustained level around 8:30–8:50.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One sketch of three
cues.text: The first movement closes before Jeux de vagues, “Play of the waves”. That separate movement replaces this broad conclusion with more fragmentary, continually changing material.
cues.evidence: The score’s movement order and the Boston Symphony programme note identify Jeux de vagues as the second sketch.

transitions.title: A new bass gives the figures direction
transitions.how: The introduction’s low B foundation gives way to the main span’s D♭ centre. Debussy gathers the separated gestures into more continuous motion, with a more flowing pulse and short rising figures above the bass. D♭ major is established through its pitch collection and repeated support rather than a Classical-style stop and restart. In Odom’s band transcription, follow the contrast between sustained wind sonorities and the smaller moving figures; the original score’s string colours are not the sounds heard here.
transitions.evidence: The main-span boundary is 1:42, a measured change following the introduction’s swell. Analysis moves from the opening B foundation to D♭-centred windows around 1:40–2:15. Debussy’s introduction/main-span design supplies the tonal and rhythmic change; the source credits Lawrence Odom’s concert-band transcription. No original string entrance or specific reassignment is claimed.

transitions.title: A♭ holds the next arrival back
transitions.how: The preceding motion contracts into a quiet stretch organised around A♭, the dominant pitch of D♭. Short figures and changing upper notes remain active, but the low foundation delays a decisive arrival on the tonic. The contrast is between a relatively stationary bass and moving detail, not between music and silence. In this wind-band version, listen below the upper gestures for the held harmonic ground that makes the later broadening audible.
transitions.evidence: The quiet-before-close boundary is 7:20, the report’s strongest change. Low A♭ persists through much of 7:20–8:05 at reduced relative level. The score’s prolonged dominant-pitch foundation supplies the harmonic interpretation; changing chroma labels are not treated as chord names. Instrumental wording is restricted to the documented band forces.

transitions.title: Small gestures become broad chordal motion
transitions.how: The quiet preparation gives way to a broader harmonic rhythm and D♭ major sonority. Instead of stopping the smaller figures, Debussy sets sustained, chordal phrases against their continuing movement: two rates of activity occupy the same passage. The bass now participates in the expanding progression rather than simply holding the earlier A♭ foundation. The band’s wind and brass weight makes the change of scale clear without requiring the string tremolos of the orchestral original.
transitions.evidence: The closing-chorale marker is 8:34, also a measured boundary. Relative level and brightness rise markedly from 8:25 into 8:35–8:50; the D♭ region around 8:35 supports the written closing destination. The score supplies the broad chordal conclusion and layered rhythmic activity. No unpublished Odom instrumental allocation or detailed chord-by-chord route is inferred; the relations file establishes no large literal reprise.

composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
